title: nmap
description: Nmap ("Network Mapper") is a free, open-source utility for network discovery and security auditing. It sends crafted packets to targets and analyzes the responses to determine which hosts are up, which ports are open, what services and versions they're running, what OS they're running, and more — via its scripting engine (NSE) it can also detect vulnerabilities and misconfigurations.

Getting Started.Getting Started:
Nmap is a command-line network scanner. This guide covers installing it on **Arch Linux**, running your first scan, and understanding the output.

## Install on Arch Linux

Nmap is in the official `extra` repository, so no AUR package is needed:

```bash
sudo pacman -S nmap
```

Verify the install and check the version:

```bash
nmap --version
```

As of this writing the current stable release is **7.991** (2026-08-06). Arch tracks upstream closely, so `pacman -Syu` will pick up new Nmap releases shortly after they're published on nmap.org.

## Your first scan

Scan a single host for its most common 1000 ports:

```bash
nmap scanme.nmap.org
```

`scanme.nmap.org` is a host the Nmap project maintains specifically for people to test scans against — you don't need permission to scan it. **Never scan hosts or networks you don't own or have explicit authorization to test**; port scanning networks without permission can violate computer-abuse laws in many jurisdictions.

Typical output looks like:

```
Starting Nmap 7.991 ( https://nmap.org ) at 2026-09-17 10:00 CEST
Nmap scan report for scanme.nmap.org (45.33.32.156)
Host is up (0.087s latency).
Not shown: 996 closed tcp ports (reset)
PORT     STATE    SERVICE
22/tcp   open     ssh
80/tcp   open     http
9929/tcp open     nping-echo
31337/tcp open    Elite

Nmap done: 1 IP address (1 host up) scanned in 4.52 seconds
```

- **PORT** — the port number and protocol (tcp/udp).
- **STATE** — `open`, `closed`, or `filtered` (a firewall is dropping probes).
- **SERVICE** — Nmap's guess at the service, from its `nmap-services` database of common port/service mappings.

## Core concepts

**Scan types** control *how* Nmap probes ports. The default without root privileges is a TCP connect scan (`-sT`); with root/CAP_NET_RAW it defaults to a SYN scan (`-sS`), which is faster and stealthier because it never completes the TCP handshake.

**Target specification** accepts hostnames, single IPs, CIDR ranges, and ranges with hyphens:

```bash
nmap 192.168.1.1                  # single IP
nmap 192.168.1.0/24               # whole subnet
nmap 192.168.1.1-50               # range
nmap -iL targets.txt              # from a file, one target per line
```

**Port specification** with `-p`:

```bash
nmap -p 22,80,443 target          # specific ports
nmap -p 1-1000 target             # range
nmap -p- target                   # all 65535 ports
nmap -F target                    # fast mode, top 100 ports
```

**Privileges matter.** Many of Nmap's most useful features — SYN scan, OS detection, some NSE scripts — need raw socket access. On Arch, run with `sudo`, or grant the binary the capability once so you don't need root every time:

```bash
sudo setcap cap_net_raw,cap_net_admin,cap_net_bind_service+eip $(which nmap)
```

Next: [Installation](/nmap/installation/) for more detail on install options, or [First Scan](/nmap/first-scan/) to go deeper on interpreting results.
Getting Started.Installation:
## Arch Linux (pacman)

```bash
sudo pacman -S nmap
```

This installs the `nmap` binary along with `ncat`, `nping`, and `ndiff`. Zenmap (the GUI) is **not** packaged for Arch — its Python 2/GTK2 dependencies were dropped from the repos years ago. If you want a GUI front-end on Arch, look at community alternatives in the AUR (e.g. `zenmap-git`, unmaintained) or just use the CLI with `--stats-every` for progress feedback on long scans.

## Building from source

If you need a newer version than what's in the Arch repos, or want custom compile flags:

```bash
curl -O https://nmap.org/dist/nmap-7.991.tar.bz2
tar xjf nmap-7.991.tar.bz2
cd nmap-7.991
./configure
make -j$(nproc)
sudo make install
```

Build dependencies on Arch: `base-devel`, `openssl`, `libpcap`, `pcre2`.

```bash
sudo pacman -S --needed base-devel openssl libpcap pcre2
```

## Verifying your install

```bash
nmap --version
```

```
Nmap version 7.991 ( https://nmap.org )
Platform: x86_64-pc-linux-gnu
Compiled with: liblua-5.4.7 openssl-3.0.21 libssh2-1.11.1_NMAP1 libz-1.3.1 libpcre2-10.47 nmap-libpcap-1.10.6 nmap-libdnet-1.18.0 ipv6
Compiled without:
Available nsock engines: epoll poll select
```

## Setting up raw-socket capabilities (optional but recommended)

Rather than prefixing every command with `sudo`, grant `nmap` the specific Linux capabilities it needs for raw packet access:

```bash
sudo setcap cap_net_raw,cap_net_admin,cap_net_bind_service+eip $(which nmap)
```

This lets your regular user run SYN scans and OS detection without full root. Note this needs to be re-applied after every package upgrade, since `pacman` replaces the binary.

## Related tools bundled with Nmap

| Tool | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `ncat` | Netcat-style reader/writer for network connections, with SSL, proxy, and broker support |
| `nping` | Packet generation and response analysis tool, good for custom probes and ping-like latency checks |
| `ndiff` | Compares two Nmap XML scan results and reports differences |

All three install alongside `nmap` from the Arch package.
Getting Started.First Scan:
This page walks through reading Nmap output in detail, using the [Getting Started](/nmap/getting-started/) example as a base.

## Port states

Nmap reports one of six port states. In practice you'll mostly see the first three:

- **open** — an application is actively accepting connections on this port.
- **closed** — the port is reachable (something responded) but nothing is listening.
- **filtered** — Nmap can't tell if the port is open, because a firewall, filter, or other obstruction is dropping probes without a response.
- **unfiltered** — reachable but Nmap can't determine open vs. closed (only seen with `-sA`, the ACK scan).
- **open|filtered** — Nmap couldn't determine if the port is open or filtered (no response received, common with UDP).
- **closed|filtered** — Nmap couldn't determine if the port is closed or filtered (only seen with the IP ID idle scan, `-sI`).

## Increasing verbosity

```bash
nmap -v scanme.nmap.org       # verbose: shows scan phases as they happen
nmap -vv scanme.nmap.org      # very verbose
nmap -d scanme.nmap.org       # debug output (very noisy)
```

## Service and version detection

Add `-sV` to have Nmap probe open ports and try to identify the actual software and version, not just the port's conventional service name:

```bash
nmap -sV scanme.nmap.org
```

```
PORT     STATE SERVICE VERSION
22/tcp   open  ssh     OpenSSH 8.9p1 Ubuntu 3ubuntu0.10 (Ubuntu Linux; protocol 2.0)
80/tcp   open  http    Apache httpd 2.4.52 ((Ubuntu))
```

This is far more useful for real assessments than the default port/service guess, since it's based on actually talking to the service rather than the port number alone.

## OS detection

`-O` attempts to fingerprint the target's operating system from subtle differences in how its TCP/IP stack responds to crafted probes. Requires elevated privileges (root or the capability shown in [Installation](/nmap/installation/)):

```bash
sudo nmap -O scanme.nmap.org
```

## Saving output

For anything beyond an interactive one-off scan, save output so you can parse or diff it later:

```bash
nmap -oN scan.txt target      # normal (human-readable) format
nmap -oX scan.xml target      # XML — best for programmatic parsing
nmap -oG scan.gnmap target    # grepable format (legacy, still handy for quick greps)
nmap -oA scan target          # all three formats at once, using "scan" as the base filename
```

XML output (`-oX`) is the format to reach for if you're going to parse results with a script — see the [dart_nmap example](/nmap/dart-nmap-parsing-xml/) in the Guides section for parsing it from Dart.

## A well-rounded "just tell me what's there" scan

A common combination for a thorough but still reasonably fast scan of a single host:

```bash
sudo nmap -sS -sV -O -p- -T4 target
```

- `-sS` SYN scan
- `-sV` version detection
- `-O` OS detection
- `-p-` all 65535 ports
- `-T4` aggressive timing (see [Timing and Performance](/nmap/timing-and-performance/))

This is much slower than a default scan since it checks every port, so expect it to take minutes rather than seconds on a typical host.

Guides.Scan Types Explained:
Nmap supports many scan techniques, selected with a single-letter flag after `-s`. This page covers the ones you'll actually use.

## TCP scans

| Flag | Name | Needs root? | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-sS` | SYN scan | Yes | The default when run as root. Sends a SYN, never completes the handshake ("half-open"). Fast and relatively stealthy. |
| `-sT` | Connect scan | No | Uses the OS's normal `connect()` call to complete a full TCP handshake. The default for non-root users. Slower and more visible in logs, but works without special privileges. |
| `-sA` | ACK scan | Yes | Doesn't determine open/closed — used to map firewall rulesets (distinguishes "filtered" from "unfiltered"). |
| `-sW` | Window scan | Yes | Like ACK scan but examines the TCP window size in RST packets to sometimes distinguish open from closed on certain stacks. |
| `-sM` | Maimon scan | Yes | Sends FIN/ACK probes; exploits a BSD-derived quirk that's mostly of historical interest today. |

## UDP scan

```bash
sudo nmap -sU target
```

UDP scanning is inherently slower and less reliable than TCP: most UDP services simply don't respond to an empty probe, so Nmap relies on ICMP port-unreachable messages (or protocol-specific payloads from `nmap-service-probes`) to distinguish `closed` from `open|filtered`. Combine with `-sV` for much better accuracy, since version detection sends protocol-appropriate payloads.

## Stealth-oriented scans

- `-sF` (FIN), `-sX` (Xmas), `-sN` (Null) — send unusual TCP flag combinations that some older/simpler firewalls and IDS won't flag as a scan. Modern stateful firewalls generally see through these; they're situational rather than a default choice.
- `-sI <zombie host>` — the idle/zombie scan, which uses a third-party "zombie" host's IP ID sequence to scan a target without ever sending a packet from your own IP. Requires finding a suitable zombie host with predictable IP ID incrementing (increasingly rare on modern systems that randomize IP IDs).

## Host discovery only

Sometimes you just want to know which hosts are alive, without port-scanning any of them:

```bash
nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24
```

`-sn` (previously called `-sP`) skips port scanning entirely and just does host discovery (ARP ping on a local network, ICMP/TCP probes otherwise).

## Skipping host discovery

Conversely, `-Pn` treats every target as online and skips the discovery phase entirely — useful against hosts that are configured to not respond to ping but do have open ports:

```bash
nmap -Pn -p 80,443 target
```

See [Firewall and IDS Evasion](/nmap/firewall-and-ids-evasion/) for more on combining these with timing controls against restrictive networks.
Guides.Timing and Performance:
Nmap's timing templates (`-T0` through `-T5`) are the simplest lever for trading speed against stealth and reliability.

| Template | Name | Use case |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-T0` | Paranoid | Extremely slow, one probe every 5 minutes. IDS evasion over long timeframes. |
| `-T1` | Sneaky | Very slow, IDS evasion. |
| `-T2` | Polite | Slows down to use less bandwidth and target resources. |
| `-T3` | Normal | **Default.** Balanced. |
| `-T4` | Aggressive | Assumes a fast, reliable network. Good for scanning your own infrastructure or well-connected targets like `scanme.nmap.org`. |
| `-T5` | Insane | Sacrifices accuracy for speed; probes may be dropped, causing false negatives on slow or lossy networks. |

`-T4` is a common, safe default for scanning targets on a reliable local or well-connected network; reach for `-T0`/`-T1` only when timing matters for evasion, since they can make even a small scan take hours.

## Fine-grained timing controls

Beyond the templates, individual timing parameters can be tuned directly:

```bash
nmap --min-rate 300 target       # send at least 300 packets/sec
nmap --max-retries 2 target      # cap retransmissions per probe
nmap --host-timeout 5m target    # give up on a host after 5 minutes
nmap --scan-delay 1s target      # wait 1s between probes to the same host
```

`--min-rate` is especially useful for large scans across many hosts — it prevents Nmap's built-in congestion control from slowing things down more than necessary when scanning networks known to handle high packet rates.

## Parallelism

```bash
nmap --min-hostgroup 50 --max-hostgroup 100 192.168.0.0/16
```

Controls how many hosts Nmap scans in parallel as a batch. Larger hostgroups speed up big scans but increase memory usage and can trigger rate-limiting or IDS alerts more readily.

## Watching progress on a long scan

```bash
nmap --stats-every 10s -p- target
```

Prints a progress line every 10 seconds — useful for full-port or large-network scans that might otherwise run silently for a long time. As of Nmap 7.991, `--stats-every` also works correctly with `--noninteractive`, so it's safe to use in scripts and CI logs, not just interactive terminals.
Guides.Using the Nmap Scripting Engine (NSE):
NSE lets Nmap run Lua scripts against scanned targets for deeper detection: vulnerability checks, brute-forcing, additional enumeration, and more. There are over 600 scripts bundled with Nmap.

## Running scripts

```bash
nmap --script=default target          # run the "default" category (safe, useful scripts)
nmap -sC target                       # shorthand for --script=default
nmap --script=vuln target             # run vulnerability-detection scripts
nmap --script=http-title target       # run one specific script by name
nmap --script=ssh* target             # run all scripts matching a glob
```

## Script categories

Scripts are tagged with one or more categories:

- `default` — safe, fast, and useful enough to run routinely (this is what `-sC` runs).
- `discovery` — network/service enumeration (e.g. `dns-brute`, `smb-enum-shares`).
- `vuln` — checks for known vulnerabilities.
- `auth` — authentication-related checks and bypasses.
- `brute` — credential brute-forcing.
- `intrusive` — may crash services or be noticeable/disruptive; not run by default.
- `safe` — unlikely to crash anything or use excessive resources.

## Script arguments

Many scripts accept arguments via `--script-args`:

```bash
nmap --script=http-enum --script-args http-enum.basepath=/api/ target
nmap --script=ssh-brute --script-args userdb=users.txt,passdb=passwords.txt target
```

## The "kitchen sink" combo

```bash
sudo nmap -sV -sC -O target
```

Version detection, default scripts, and OS detection together is a common baseline for a thorough single-host assessment.

## Finding scripts

Every script is documented at nmap.org's NSE doc pages, and locally:

```bash
ls /usr/share/nmap/scripts/ | grep http
nmap --script-help=ssh-brute
```

## A note on ethics and legality

Several NSE scripts (brute-force, vulnerability exploitation checks) are intrusive by design. Only run `vuln`, `brute`, `exploit`, or `intrusive` category scripts against systems you own or are explicitly authorized to test — the same rule that applies to scanning generally applies with extra weight here, since some of these scripts can crash services or trigger account lockouts.
Guides.Firewall and IDS Evasion:
Nmap includes several techniques for probing networks protected by firewalls or intrusion detection systems. These are for **authorized security testing** — using them against systems you don't have permission to test is illegal in most jurisdictions.

## Fragmenting packets

```bash
sudo nmap -f target            # fragment probes into 8-byte chunks
sudo nmap -f -f target         # 16-byte chunks
sudo nmap --mtu 24 target      # custom fragment size (multiple of 8)
```

Some older packet-filtering devices and IDS signatures fail to reassemble fragments before inspection, letting probes slip through undetected. Modern stateful firewalls generally reassemble before filtering, so this is far less effective than it once was.

## Decoys

```bash
sudo nmap -D decoy1,decoy2,ME,decoy3 target
```

Sends scan probes that appear to come from multiple spoofed source addresses in addition to your real one (`ME`), making it harder for the target to tell which source actually performed the scan. `-D RND:10` generates 10 random decoy addresses.

## Source port spoofing

```bash
sudo nmap --source-port 53 target
```

Some old firewall configurations trust traffic from specific "well-known" source ports (like 53/DNS or 20/FTP-data) without proper stateful inspection. Setting the source port to one of these can bypass such rules.

## Spoofing the source IP / MAC

```bash
sudo nmap -S <spoofed-IP> -e eth0 -Pn target      # spoof source IP (you won't see replies)
sudo nmap --spoof-mac 0 target                    # random MAC address
sudo nmap --spoof-mac Apple target                # random MAC with Apple's vendor prefix
```

Spoofing the source IP means Nmap can't receive replies (since they go to the spoofed address), so this is mainly useful combined with the idle scan (`-sI`) or for triggering firewall/IDS log noise.

## Combining with timing

Slow timing templates (`-T0`, `-T1`, see [Timing and Performance](/nmap/timing-and-performance/)) reduce the chance of tripping rate-based IDS alerts, at the cost of the scan taking dramatically longer — a full `-T0` scan of even a handful of ports can take hours.

## Realistic expectations

Modern network security has moved well past what these techniques were originally designed to defeat. Treat evasion techniques as tools for testing whether your own defenses actually catch them, not as a way to guarantee an undetected scan against a competent, actively monitored network.

Project.About & Changelog:
## About

Nmap ("Network Mapper") was first released by Gordon Lyon (aka "Fyodor") in September 1997, originally described in a Phrack Magazine article. It's now maintained by Lyon along with a community of contributors, and remains free and open source under the Nmap Public Source License (NPSL).

Alongside the core scanner, the project maintains:

- **Ncat** — a modern, feature-rich Netcat replacement (SSL, proxying, IPv6, broker mode)
- **Nping** — packet generation and network measurement tool
- **Ndiff** — compares two XML scan results
- **Npcap** — the packet-capture driver Nmap uses on Windows (replacing the long-abandoned WinPcap)

Zenmap, the official GUI, is still available from the project but as of recent releases is distributed as a Python wheel rather than platform-specific installers, and is not currently packaged for Arch Linux (see [Installation](/nmap/installation/)).

## Recent release history

| Version | Date | Highlights |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 7.991 | 2026-08-06 | Security fixes across libssh2 (multiple CVEs), OpenSSL upgraded to 3.0.21, numerous NSE and Ncat bug fixes |
| 7.99 | 2026-03-26 | Updated OS/service fingerprint database, Npcap upgraded to 1.87, Zenmap now distributed as a universal Python wheel |
| 7.98 | 2025-08-21 | Security fix for the Windows installer (CVE-2025-43715, an NSIS privilege-escalation issue), several DNS-resolver stability fixes |
| 7.97 | 2025-05-12 | Zenmap crash fixes on Windows, forward-DNS resolver fix for `/etc/hosts` and `localhost` |
| 7.96 | 2025-05-01 | Forward DNS lookups parallelized (dramatic speedup for large hostname lists), Npcap upgraded to 1.82, Zenmap dark mode added |

For the complete, authoritative changelog going back to Nmap's earliest releases, see the [official Nmap Changelog](https://nmap.org/changelog.html).

## Licensing

Nmap is distributed under the Nmap Public Source License (NPSL), a GPLv2-derived license with additional terms specific to Nmap's distribution model. Commercial redistribution (bundling Nmap inside a closed-source product) generally requires an Nmap OEM license — see the project's [OEM program page](https://nmap.org/oem) for details. Using, modifying, and redistributing Nmap under the standard open-source terms does not require any special license.
Project.FAQ:
### Is it legal to use Nmap?

Nmap itself is completely legal software. What can be illegal, depending on your jurisdiction, is running scans against networks or hosts you don't own and don't have explicit authorization to test. Always get written permission before scanning infrastructure that isn't yours — this includes scanning "just to check" a friend's network, a public Wi-Fi network you're connected to, or third-party cloud infrastructure without going through the cloud provider's scanning-authorization process (AWS, GCP, and Azure all require prior authorization for certain kinds of scans).

### Why do I need root/sudo for some scans?

Techniques like SYN scan (`-sS`) and OS detection (`-O`) construct raw packets by hand rather than going through the OS's normal socket API, which requires elevated privileges on Linux (`CAP_NET_RAW`). See [Installation](/nmap/installation/) for how to grant this capability to the binary directly instead of using `sudo` every time.

### My scan is taking forever — how do I speed it up?

Start with [Timing and Performance](/nmap/timing-and-performance/). Common quick wins: use `-T4` instead of the default `-T3`, don't scan all 65535 ports (`-p-`) unless you actually need to, and skip `-Pn` unless you know host discovery is being blocked (skipping discovery unnecessarily means Nmap will fully port-scan hosts that are actually down).

### Why does UDP scanning seem so unreliable?

This is inherent to UDP itself, not a Nmap limitation: there's no handshake, so Nmap can only infer a port's state from whether it gets an ICMP unreachable message back (closed) or nothing at all (open|filtered — Nmap genuinely can't distinguish the two without a protocol-specific probe). Adding `-sV` significantly improves accuracy since Nmap will send protocol-appropriate payloads for many common UDP services rather than an empty packet.

### Does Nmap have a pure-Dart or pure-any-non-C++ implementation?

No — Nmap itself is a C++ codebase, and there's no official reimplementation in Dart or other languages. For Dart projects, the practical approach is shelling out to the installed `nmap` binary and parsing its XML output; see [Parsing Nmap XML Output](/nmap/dart-nmap-parsing-xml/) in the Guides section.

### Where do I report a bug or request a feature?

The project tracks issues on GitHub at [github.com/nmap/nmap](https://github.com/nmap/nmap/issues). Security-sensitive reports should go through the process described on [nmap.org](https://nmap.org).
Project.License: Nmap is released under a custom license, the **Nmap Public Source License**, based on GPLv2 with additional clauses (notably restrictions on how Nmap can be bundled into commercial or closed products, and a requirement that modifications be released as source). It is *not* plain vanilla GPL, so double-check the [official licensing page](https://nmap.org/book/man-legal.html) before bundling Nmap into a commercial product. CLI Reference.CLI Reference: Overview:
Nmap's full option list is extensive (`man nmap` or `nmap -h` for the authoritative source). This section groups the options you'll reach for most often.

| Page | Covers |
| --- | --- |
| [Target Specification](/nmap/target-specification/) | How to specify hosts, ranges, and exclusions |
| [Scan Techniques](/nmap/cli-scan-techniques/) | The `-s*` flags |
| [Port Options](/nmap/port-options/) | `-p`, `-F`, `--top-ports`, etc. |
| [Output Options](/nmap/output-options/) | `-o*` flags and verbosity |

For the complete, canonical option reference straight from the source, see `nmap -h` or the man page shipped with your install (`man nmap`).
CLI Reference.Target Specification:
```bash
nmap 192.168.1.1                    # single IP
nmap 192.168.1.1 192.168.1.2        # multiple targets
nmap scanme.nmap.org                # hostname (resolved via DNS)
nmap 192.168.1.0/24                 # CIDR notation
nmap 192.168.1.1-254                # range (last octet)
nmap 192.168.1-5.1-254              # ranges in multiple octets
nmap -iL targets.txt                # read targets from a file
nmap -iR 100                        # scan 100 random public IPs
nmap --exclude 192.168.1.5          # exclude a host from an otherwise broader target spec
nmap --excludefile exclude.txt      # exclude hosts listed in a file
```

Target files (`-iL`) take one target per line, and accept any of the formats above (hostnames, IPs, CIDR, ranges) mixed together in the same file. Comments starting with `#` are ignored.

`-iR` (random targets) is intended for internet-wide research scanning and should only be used with a clear understanding of the legal and ethical implications of scanning hosts you have no relationship with — most such targets belong to third parties who have not consented to being scanned.
CLI Reference.CLI Scan Techniques:
Quick reference for scan-type flags — see [Scan Types Explained](/nmap/scan-types-explained/) in the Guides section for the full explanation of each.

```bash
-sS   SYN scan (default w/ root)
-sT   Connect scan (default w/o root)
-sU   UDP scan
-sA   ACK scan
-sW   Window scan
-sM   Maimon scan
-sN   Null scan
-sF   FIN scan
-sX   Xmas scan
-sI <zombie>   Idle/zombie scan
-sO   IP protocol scan
-sn   Host discovery only (no port scan)
-Pn   Skip host discovery, treat all hosts as online
```

Combine `-sS` and `-sU` in the same invocation to scan both TCP and UDP in one pass:

```bash
sudo nmap -sS -sU -p T:80,443,U:53,123 target
```

The `T:`/`U:` prefixes in `-p` let you specify different port lists per protocol in a combined scan.
CLI Reference.Port Options:
```bash
-p 22                    # single port
-p 22,80,443             # comma-separated list
-p 1-1000                # range
-p-                      # all 65535 ports
-p U:53,T:21-25          # protocol-specific port lists (see below)
-F                       # fast mode: top 100 ports only
--top-ports 20           # scan the N most common ports per nmap-services
--port-ratio 0.1         # scan ports with a frequency ratio above this threshold
-r                       # scan ports in numeric order rather than a randomized order
```

By default Nmap randomizes port scan order per host to reduce detectability and avoid overloading a target with sequential probes; `-r` disables this when deterministic ordering is useful (e.g. for reproducible test logs).
CLI Reference.Output Options:
```bash
-oN file.txt      # normal output
-oX file.xml      # XML output
-oG file.gnmap    # grepable output (legacy)
-oA basename      # all formats at once, using "basename" for each extension
-v                # verbose
-vv               # more verbose
-d                # debug
--reason          # show the reason a port is in a given state (e.g. "syn-ack" vs "no-response")
--open            # only show open (or possibly-open) ports in output
--stats-every 10s # periodic progress updates during long scans
--append-output   # append to output file instead of overwriting
--noninteractive  # disable runtime keyboard interaction (useful in scripts/CI)
```

For any output that will be consumed by another program (including a Dart script — see [Parsing Nmap XML Output](/nmap/dart-nmap-parsing-xml/)), prefer `-oX` over `-oN`/`-oG`: it's the only format with a documented, stable schema.
CLI Reference.Host Discovery & DNS:
## Ping / host-discovery types

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-sn` | Host discovery only, no port scan |
| `-Pn` | Skip host discovery entirely, treat every target as online |
| `-PE` | ICMP echo request discovery |
| `-PP` | ICMP timestamp request discovery |
| `-PM` | ICMP netmask request discovery |
| `-PS PORTS` | TCP SYN discovery on given ports |
| `-PA PORTS` | TCP ACK discovery on given ports |
| `-PU PORTS` | UDP discovery on given ports |
| `-PY PORTS` | SCTP INIT discovery on given ports |
| `-PO PROTOCOLS` | IP protocol ping |
| `--traceroute` | Trace the network path to each target |

## DNS resolution

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-n` | Never do reverse DNS resolution (faster) |
| `-R` | Always do reverse DNS resolution, even for non-responsive hosts |
| `--dns-servers SERVERS` | Use specific DNS servers instead of the system default |
| `--system-dns` | Use the OS's own resolver instead of Nmap's built-in parallel resolver |
| `--resolve-all` | Scan every resolved address for a hostname, not just the first |

## IPv6 and protocol

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-6` | Enable IPv6 scanning |
| `-sO` | IP protocol scan (which IP protocols, not ports, respond) |
CLI Reference.OS & Version Detection:
| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-O` | Enable OS detection |
| `--osscan-guess`, `--fuzzy` | Guess OS more aggressively when there's no exact match |
| `--max-os-tries N` | Limit OS-detection attempts against an unresponsive host |
| `-sV` | Enable service/version detection |
| `--version-intensity N` | Probe intensity `0`-`9` (higher = more thorough, slower) |
| `--version-light` | Alias for `--version-intensity 2` (fast) |
| `--version-all` | Alias for `--version-intensity 9` (try every probe) |
| `--version-trace` | Show detailed version-detection activity, for debugging a misidentification |
| `-A` | Aggressive: enables `-O -sV -sC --traceroute` together |

`-A` is convenient for a quick, thorough look at a single host you're authorized to test, but it's also the loudest, slowest, and most fingerprintable option combination — not the right default for a stealthy or large-scale scan.
CLI Reference.Timing Templates & Rate Control:
## Timing templates

| Flag | Speed | Use case |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-T0` | Paranoid | IDS evasion, extremely slow (5min+ between probes) |
| `-T1` | Sneaky | IDS evasion, very slow |
| `-T2` | Polite | Slower, less bandwidth/target load |
| `-T3` | Normal | Default |
| `-T4` | Aggressive | Fast, assumes a reliable, reasonably fast network |
| `-T5` | Insane | Fastest, sacrifices accuracy for speed |

## Fine-grained rate/parallelism control

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `--min-rate N` | Send at least N packets per second |
| `--max-rate N` | Never exceed N packets per second |
| `--min-parallelism N` / `--max-parallelism N` | Bound concurrent probe count |
| `--min-rtt-timeout` / `--max-rtt-timeout` / `--initial-rtt-timeout` | Bound how long Nmap waits for a probe response before retrying |
| `--max-retries N` | Cap probe retransmissions per port |
| `--host-timeout TIME` | Give up on a host entirely after this long |
| `--scan-delay TIME` / `--max-scan-delay TIME` | Force a minimum delay between probes (throttling, gentler on the target) |
| `--stats-every TIME` | Periodic progress output during a long scan |

`-T4` with explicit `--min-rate`/`--max-rate` tuning is common for scanning a network you administer where you know the bandwidth budget; the paranoid templates (`-T0`/`-T1`) exist mainly for authorized red-team engagements where detection avoidance is explicitly in scope.
CLI Reference.Evasion & Spoofing Flags:
These exist for legitimate purposes — testing your own firewall/IDS rules, or an authorized red-team engagement — and are covered conceptually in [Firewall and IDS Evasion](/nmap/firewall-and-ids-evasion/).

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-f` | Fragment packets into smaller pieces |
| `--mtu N` | Set a custom fragment size (multiple of 8) |
| `-D decoy1,decoy2,...,ME` | Scan alongside spoofed decoy source addresses, hiding your real one among them |
| `-S SPOOFED-IP` | Spoof the source address entirely (usually only useful with `-e` and if you control the reply path) |
| `-e INTERFACE` | Use a specific network interface |
| `-g PORT`, `--source-port PORT` | Use a fixed source port (some legacy firewalls trust traffic from certain ports, e.g. 53 or 20) |
| `--data-length N` | Append random data to reach a specific packet length |
| `--spoof-mac MAC|VENDOR|0` | Spoof the MAC address on Ethernet scans |
| `--badsum` | Send packets with an intentionally invalid checksum (to see if a target's stack drops or accepts them, revealing a naive implementation) |
| `--ttl N` | Set a specific IP time-to-live |
CLI Reference.NSE Flags:
See [Using the Nmap Scripting Engine (NSE)](/nmap/using-the-nmap-scripting-engine-nse/) for the conceptual walkthrough; this is the flag reference.

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-sC` | Run the default script set (alias for `--script=default`) |
| `--script CATEGORY\|NAME\|PATH` | Run specific script(s), a category (`default`, `vuln`, `safe`, `discovery`, ...), or comma-separated combination |
| `--script-args ARGS` | Pass `key=value` arguments to scripts (comma-separated) |
| `--script-args-file FILE` | Load script arguments from a file instead of the command line |
| `--script-help NAME` | Show a script's description and accepted arguments |
| `--script-trace` | Show all data sent/received by scripts, for debugging |
| `--script-updatedb` | Rebuild the script database after adding/removing `.nse` files |

```bash
nmap --script vuln 192.168.1.1
nmap --script http-title --script-args http.useragent="MyAgent" 192.168.1.1
```

Learn by Examples.Auditing Your Home Lab, Then Parsing The:
A home lab has a router, a NAS, a couple of Raspberry Pis, and a laptop — all on one subnet you own. This walkthrough runs a realistic, complete nmap audit of that network, then feeds the structured output into a small Dart script, tying together nearly every concept in this doc.

## 1. Confirm scope

```bash
ip addr show | grep 'inet '
```

Confirms the actual subnet before scanning anything — e.g. `192.168.1.0/24`. Never guess a target range; scanning outside your own network without authorization is exactly the line this tool's legal notes warn about.

## 2. Host discovery first, before any port scanning

```bash
sudo nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24
```

`-sn` just finds who's alive on the network — a fast first pass before spending time port-scanning hosts that don't even exist.

## 3. A quick top-ports scan across everything found

```bash
sudo nmap -F -T4 192.168.1.0/24 -oA quick-scan
```

`-F` (fast mode, top 100 ports) with `-T4` (aggressive timing, fine on a home LAN) gives a same-minute overview; `-oA` writes all three output formats (`.nmap`, `.xml`, `.gnmap`) under the `quick-scan` basename in one go.

## 4. Full port range and version detection on one interesting host

Say the NAS at `192.168.1.50` stood out:

```bash
sudo nmap -p- -sV --version-intensity 5 -O 192.168.1.50 -oX nas-full.xml
```

`-p-` scans all 65535 ports, `-sV` identifies what's actually running on each open one, `-O` attempts OS fingerprinting — and `-oX` is used specifically because this result is about to be parsed programmatically, not just read.

## 5. Run default + vuln scripts against your own device

```bash
sudo nmap -sV -sC --script vuln 192.168.1.50 -oX nas-vuln.xml
```

`-sC` (default script set) plus `--script vuln` (known-vulnerability checks) — reasonable on a device you own and want to harden, and exactly the kind of thing to run *before* exposing a NAS to the internet, not after.

## 6. Check the router's firewall rules by testing from outside its LACL

```bash
sudo nmap -sA -p 1-1000 192.168.1.1
```

An ACK scan (`-sA`) against your own router helps confirm which ports are actually filtered by its firewall versus simply closed — different `nmap` scan types answer different security questions, and this one is specifically about firewall rule behavior, not "what's listening."

## 7. Parse the XML results in Dart

With `nas-full.xml` and `nas-vuln.xml` in hand, this is where the [Dart: Parsing Nmap XML Output](/nmap/dart-nmap-parsing-xml/) guide's approach comes in directly:

```bash
dart run bin/summarize_scan.dart nas-full.xml
```

A small Dart script (per that guide's `xml` package approach) reads the file, walks `<host>` → `<ports>` → `<port>` elements, and prints a summary like:

```
192.168.1.50: 4 open ports
  22/tcp  ssh     OpenSSH 9.6
  80/tcp  http    nginx 1.26.0
  443/tcp https   nginx 1.26.0
  5000/tcp http   Synology DSM
```

## 8. Turn it into a recurring, scripted check

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
sudo nmap -sV -T4 192.168.1.0/24 -oX "/var/log/nmap/scan-$(date +%F).xml" \
  --stats-every 30s
dart run bin/diff_scans.dart /var/log/nmap/scan-*.xml
```

A cron job running this weekly, with a Dart script comparing successive XML files, turns one-off manual auditing into an ongoing "did anything new start listening on my network" check — a genuinely useful home-lab habit built entirely from tools covered in this doc.

## What this walkthrough covered

`-sn` discovery, `-F` and `-p-` port scanning, `-sV`/`-O` detection, `-oA`/`-oX` output formats, `-sC`/`--script vuln` NSE usage, `-sA` for firewall-behavior testing, `-T4` timing, and closing the loop by parsing `-oX` output in Dart for both a one-off summary and a recurring automated diff — the realistic end-to-end shape of using nmap on infrastructure you actually own.
